issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette:
Arjun is a 24-year-old South Asian man currently employed as a junior diplomat, a role he accepted with considerable pride less than two years before the events that brought him to seek clinical help. He is in a relationship, though he describes it with a flatness that suggests the connection has become more obligation than comfort. His PCL-5 score of 66 places him in the severe range, and the picture that has emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a young man who has not so much survived a war zone as been quietly dismantled by it.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Arjun was stationed at a diplomatic post in a city that came under sustained aerial bombardment. During one afternoon that he returns to repeatedly in session, a series of explosions struck within blocks of his building. He had been in a meeting room when the first blast hit; the windows blew inward, and in the chaos that followed, armed men entered the compound. What Arjun cannot fully articulate - and he is acutely aware of this failure - is what happened in the minutes after. He knows, in the way one knows facts on a page, that he was held at gunpoint, that a colleague was badly injured beside him, that there was the sharp, unmistakable smell of alcohol on the breath of one of the men who stood over him. He knows all of this. But the words, he says, dissolve before they reach his mouth. What remains instead is sensory and immediate: the smell, the sound, the feeling of being utterly exposed.

Back in Washington, where he has been reassigned to a desk role, Arjun's working days are structured and ostensibly safe - and yet the embassy corridors, the security briefings, the occasional ceremonial gathering where strangers approach with extended hands have become a sustained ordeal. When a door slams in an adjacent office, or when a delivery truck backfires on the street outside, the explosion is not remembered so much as re-entered. His body floods with the certainty that it is happening again - the flashback arriving not as image but as total re-immersion - and from that state of hyperarousal, the vivid, sensory-laden memory reasserts itself with full force, the smell of alcohol returning as though the man were standing beside him again. These triggers - the bang, the smell, the subtler but equally destabilising feeling of emotional vulnerability that descends without warning - feed directly into a sense of threat that Arjun finds impossible to reason away. Even when colleagues or his partner tell him he is safe, something in him cannot receive it. Strangers approaching his desk, couriers arriving at the building entrance, anyone moving toward him in an unannounced way - all of it registers as danger. The activated memory, so vivid and olfactorily alive, keeps the nervous system persuaded that the past is still present, and the felt sense of threat in turn pulls the memory forward again, a current that runs in both directions.

What has calcified around this cycle is a set of beliefs that Arjun holds about himself and the world with quiet, devastating conviction. He has come to believe that there is something about him - some quality he cannot name but feels responsible for - that made the event happen. He has lost whatever faith he once carried in people, in the structures of diplomacy he entered with idealism, in any sense that the future holds something worth moving toward. He sees no future for himself in any concrete sense. These appraisals do not sit passively; they sharpen his vigilance, making every ambiguous social encounter feel confirming rather than neutral, and they pull triggers closer - the feeling of vulnerability becomes more frequent, more unbearable, because he already believes himself to be fundamentally exposed.

To manage what he cannot resolve, Arjun has constructed a set of routines that have gradually taken over. He takes drugs - he is matter-of-fact about this - to blunt the evenings. He exercises compulsively, pushing past pain in a way he describes as the only time he feels he has any control over his body. He wears concealing clothing when he goes out, a deliberate effort to pass unnoticed through public space. These strategies offer brief relief, but under intoxication the memory surfaces with less resistance, and the physical depletion from excessive exercise leaves him more emotionally raw, more easily triggered, more certain the threat is real.

What finally brought Arjun in was his partner's quiet statement that she no longer recognised him. He came not with hope exactly, but with the exhausted acknowledgment that what he is doing is not working - and beneath that, barely voiced, the fear that nothing will.
